nameStory: The 'orange-cored' part of this lichen's name comes from the bright orange-red color hidden inside its reproductive structures called pycnidia - tiny bumps that look like black dots on the surface. When you scratch or break these open (gently!), they reveal a surprising burst of orange color underneath. The 'shadow' part refers to how these lichens often grow in partially shaded spots rather than full sun.
description: Orange-cored Shadow Lichen is a crusty, flat lichen that forms grayish patches on tree bark and rocks. It creates irregular, somewhat circular colonies that can spread 2-4 inches across, with a surface that looks like it's been dusted with flour. The most distinctive feature is the tiny black dots (pycnidia) scattered across its surface that contain bright orange material inside. Like all lichens, it's actually two organisms living together - a fungus and an algae working as a team.

idTips.label: Orange-cored pycnidia
idTips.description: Look for tiny black dots scattered across the gray surface - when gently scratched with a fingernail, they reveal bright orange-red contents that may stain your nail

idTips.label: Powdery gray surface
idTips.description: The main body has a dusty, flour-like texture that feels slightly rough to the touch and may leave a grayish residue on your finger

idTips.label: Irregular patches
idTips.description: Forms somewhat circular but often irregular colonies with fuzzy, indistinct edges that blend into the bark

idTips.label: Bark preference
idTips.description: Almost always found on tree bark rather than rocks, particularly favoring trees with slightly rough or furrowed bark texture

habitat: Orange-cored Shadow Lichen thrives on the bark of deciduous trees throughout New England's forests, particularly maples, oaks, and ash trees. It prefers spots with partial shade and good air circulation, often found at eye level on tree trunks in mixed hardwood forests. You'll rarely find it in heavily polluted urban areas, as it's somewhat sensitive to air quality.

seasonality.spring: Most visible after spring rains when the lichen body swells slightly and the gray color becomes more pronounced. Pycnidia may be more prominent during this active growing season.
seasonality.summer: Can appear somewhat faded or dustier in dry summer conditions, but the orange cores in the pycnidia remain bright and are easiest to detect during warm weather.
seasonality.fall: Often most noticeable in fall when leaves drop and expose more bark surface. The contrast between the gray lichen and darkened wet bark makes identification easier.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round but may appear less distinct against snow-covered or frost-covered bark. The orange pycnidial contents are still detectable even in cold weather.

funFact: This lichen is like nature's hidden highlighter - what looks like boring gray fuzz on bark actually contains dozens of tiny orange ink wells that have been used by some Indigenous peoples as a source of dye for coloring materials.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other gray, crusty lichens on bark, but the orange pycnidial cores are usually diagnostic - other similar lichens typically have white, yellow, or colorless contents in their reproductive structures. Memory trick: 'Orange-cored = scratch and explore!'
contextualKnowledge: The term 'shadow lichen' can be confusing because it doesn't mean these lichens grow in deep shade - they actually prefer partial shade with some filtered light. The 'shadow' refers more to their often subtle, grayish appearance that can blend into the shadows and textures of tree bark.
compareHints: Among its Phaeophyscia relatives, Orange-cored Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its bright orange pycnidial contents - most other wreath lichens in this genus have white, yellow, or red cores instead. The Powder-tipped Shadow Lichen looks similar but has white powdery tips on its structures, while the Red-cored Starburst has a more distinctly lobed, star-like growth pattern rather than irregular patches.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the shadow lichens in its genus, Pom-pom Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its small size and abundant powdery soredia clusters.
Among its wreath lichen relatives, Powder-tipped Shadow Lichen is distinguished by having the white soredia concentrated specifically at the lobe tips rather than scattered across the surface.
